title: Vance & Kinder x Ghostbird Content Interview

summary.short_summary: Follow-up call: Marisol finished her half marathon (with a mid-race cramping story) and the finish-line photo is ready to use. The ERP system migration hit a near-miss shipping error, caught manually by a warehouse lead; instead of hiding it, Marisol proactively emailed top accounts about the transition, which was well received. A related 8% price increase (steel tariffs) was also handled with a transparent letter to customers, again landing well apart from one lost small account. New rep Colton closed his first cold-LinkedIn deal. Marisol is considering a bigger-than-usual holiday gesture for her top twenty accounts for Q4 content.

sentences.text: Hey! How'd the half marathon go?
I finished! Barely. I cramped so bad at mile ten I thought Dave was going to have to carry me.
Did he offer?
He offered. I told him if he touched me I'd never speak to him again, out of pure stubbornness I finished on my own two feet.
Perfect, we already have that photo from you, so that one's basically ready to go. Okay, business update, how'd the ERP rollout end up? Disaster or win?
Honestly, a little of both, but it turned into a good story. We had a two day window where the new system and old system were both half working, and we almost shipped an order to the wrong facility.
Oh no.

We caught it, but only because our warehouse lead double-checked manually out of habit. So instead of pretending it was seamless, I just sent an email to our top accounts saying, hey, we're switching systems, there might be a hiccup or two this month, here's who to call directly if anything looks off.
How'd that land?
Way better than I expected. Two different customers wrote back just saying thanks for the heads up, one of them said most of their vendors would never admit something like that.
That's such a good leadership story, the value of just telling people the truth before they find out the hard way.
Yeah, my dad actually used to say something like bad news doesn't get better with age, and I finally understood what he meant by that.
Okay, love that line, we're using it. What else, didn't you also raise prices this quarter?
We did, eight percent, because of the tariff stuff on steel. I was honestly dreading those calls.
How'd it go?

Same thing, I think. I sent a short letter explaining exactly why, showed the actual cost increase we were absorbing, and didn't try to hide behind vague language like market conditions. We lost one small account over it, but a couple of the bigger ones actually thanked us for being upfront instead of quietly padding invoices like some of our competitors do.
That's a really strong pairing actually, the price increase story and the ERP story, both are basically the same lesson, transparency wins loyalty even when the news isn't great.
Never thought about it that way, but yeah.
Anything with Colton? I remember he had his first close last time.
He's doing great. He actually just closed his first deal that came from a cold LinkedIn message, no warm intro at all.
That's awesome, especially since your LinkedIn presence is part of why that lead probably trusted the company enough to respond.
I hadn't connected that dot, but that's probably true.
Okay, one more thing before we wrap. Q4 is coming up, any specific ideas you've been sitting on?
I've been wanting to do something for our top twenty customers around the holidays, more than just a card. Not sure what yet.
We can brainstorm that separately, but it could actually make a good post too, behind the scenes of what we're sending our best customers this year, that kind of thing, once you land on it.
I like that. Okay let's do that.
Great, so to recap, the ERP transparency story, the price increase story, and the Colton LinkedIn close. I'll have drafts to you by Thursday.
Perfect, thank you Jarrich.
Thanks Marisol, talk soon!
